newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU to dominate EU finance ministers meeting.
newsitem.headline: EMU to dominate EU finance ministers meeting.

text.p: European Union finance ministers meet on Sunday evening to discuss a turbulent fortnight that has thrown the future of the EU's single currency into doubt.
The ministers will meet at a dinner in Luxembourg which was originally arranged to allow them to discuss the design for new euro coins.
But the evening session and the ministers' regular monthly meeting to follow on Monday have been overshadowed by turmoil in the 15-nation bloc's plans for economic and monetary union (EMU).
"The job...will be to absorb the shocks and sparks of the last fortnight," said on EU diplomat. "The message coming out will be that we are continuing our work on EMU."
Sunday's meeting will be the first between German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and his counterparts since Bonn floated the idea of revaluing gold reserves to shore up Germany's flagging finances.
It was a move that raised questions about Germany's ability to meet the strict tests of EMU without resorting to creative accounting, something Bonn had sharply criticised others for attempting.
A compromise has been reached between Waigel and the Bundesbank, which vehemently opposed the plan, but Germany's difficulty in meeting EMU criteria has been given a clear public viewing.
The ministerial meeting will also be the first attended by new French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn, appointed following the election triumph by France's Socialist-led left.
The Socialists have made clear they want an end to the austerity programme their predecessors felt was necessary for France to meet the EMU tests.

In addition, the French Socialists indicated during the campaign that they were unhappy with the so-called Stability Pact, a hard-fought agreement between EU countries designed to keep budget deficits lean after EMU begins.
France has not yet asked to renegotiate the pact, which is due to be formally nodded through by EU leaders at a summit in Amsterdam next week.
French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has also said it is too soon to give his government's opinion on EMU or the pact.
EU diplomats dismiss some of the Socialists' comments as campaign rhetoric and say France remains one of the keenest advocates of the single currency.

But the turmoil of the past weeks has left financial and political analysts predicting that EMU will either be delayed from its January 1, 1999 start or will begin with a weaker currency in a broad range of countries.
Officials have been quick to say that there is no likelihood of a delay and that all remains on track.
Waigel said on Friday that Germany would meet the EMU criteria, taking additional budgetary measures necessary to get the deficit down to the required three percent of Gross Domestic Product.
Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, whose country is EU president until it hands over to Luxembourg in July 1, said on Saturday there was a great deal of political will behind EMU.
"There is absolutely no reason to speculate about a change of dates at the end of the Amsterdam summit," he told reporters in Madrid.
